hints: Focus on what temperature actually changes in a Boltzmann distribution, the spread of molecular energies, not the energy barrier itself.
Remember that at higher temperature the peak gets lower, shifts to higher energy, and the curve gets broader, but the total area stays the same.
Check which diagram keeps Ea in the same place on the energy axis while showing a flatter, right-shifted peak with more molecules past Ea.
walkthrough:
**Recall what Ea depends on**

Think of $E_a$ as the height of the energy barrier for the reaction. It depends on the reaction pathway, not on temperature.

Rule: $$E_a \text{ at } T_2 = E_a \text{ at } T_1$$

**Recall what temperature does to the distribution**

At higher temperature, molecules have more average kinetic energy. Fewer molecules have very low energy, and more have high energy.

So the curve starts at the origin in the same way, but the peak shifts right to higher energy, gets lower, and the tail gets fatter. Total area under the curve is constant because total number of molecules is unchanged.

**Apply to T2 and pick the shape**

We need the same $E_a$ position on the x-axis, with a lower, broader, right-shifted peak. That means a much larger fraction of molecules is now to the right of $E_a$.

Only one diagram shows all three features together: unchanged $E_a$, lower peak shifted right, and larger area beyond $E_a$.

options.A: Correct. The peak is lower and shifted to higher energy, the curve is broader, and Ea stays at the same energy value. The area to the right of Ea is clearly larger, which explains the faster rate at T2.
options.B: Incorrect. The peak has shifted so far right that Ea is now to the left of the peak. That would mean most molecules already have energy greater than Ea, which is unrealistic for a small temperature rise. It exaggerates the temperature effect.
options.C: Incorrect. This curve is essentially unchanged from T1, with a high narrow peak well to the left of Ea. It shows no temperature effect at all, so it cannot represent the higher temperature T2.
options.D: Incorrect. Here the peak looks similar to T1 but Ea has moved left to lower energy, closer to the peak. Temperature does not lower Ea, a catalyst does that. This confuses the effect of a catalyst with the effect of temperature.
